148.title: Music, tattoos, and scholars who differ
148.hook: two everyday questions where Muslim scholars genuinely disagree, and what to do with a disagreement
148.howItsDone: On contested questions like music and tattoos, many Muslims follow the view of their school, a local imam or a scholar they trust; some avoid instruments and listen to voice-only nasheeds, others listen to music with clean words.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mushtabihat, the gray area, and the itch in the chest. Your line was leave what makes you doubt. Today, two questions many people file in that drawer. Day one hundred forty-eight.

Two questions turn up in almost every Muslim group chat sooner or later. One: is music haram? Usually asked by someone with headphones on. Two: are tattoos haram? Sometimes asked by someone who already has one, and is quietly wondering whether their prayers count. The internet answers both with total confidence, in both directions. The honest answer is that scholars have disagreed, carefully, for a very long time. Today: ikhtilaf.
screen: `IS MUSIC HARAM?` → `ARE TATTOOS HARAM?` → `THE INTERNET IS VERY SURE.`

segments.voice: Ikhtilaf means disagreement, and in Islamic law it isn't a scandal. It's a field of study. Scholars working from the same Qur'an and hadith can reach different rulings, and the tradition kept their views side by side. Day three hundred seven goes deeper. Here are two examples. Music first. Many classical scholars, across the four Sunni schools, held that musical instruments are not allowed, pointing to a hadith in Bukhari that warns of people who will treat instruments as lawful. Other scholars questioned that hadith's chain or its meaning: Ibn Hazm in Spain, and, with conditions, al-Ghazali, allowed singing and some instruments when the words and the setting are clean. Nearly all allow the daff, the frame drum, at weddings, and you met the two girls singing on Eid on day one hundred twenty-seven. Many Muslims today choose voice-only nasheeds as a middle road. Then tattoos. Most Sunni scholars hold that a permanent tattoo is forbidden, citing a hadith in Bukhari that curses the one who tattoos and the one who is tattooed. Many Shia jurists see it differently, and allow tattoos whose content is decent. And on the worry that keeps people up at night, there's wide agreement: if you already have one, from before you practiced or before you knew, your wudu and your prayer count. Many scholars say there's no need to remove it, and nearly all say not if removing it would cause harm. So what do you do with a disagreement? The tradition's answer: don't grab the easiest view, or the loudest one, and don't sneer at people who follow the other. Ask a teacher you trust, and ask why.
screen: `IKHTILAF: VIEWS KEPT SIDE BY SIDE.` · `MUSIC: MANY FORBID, SOME ALLOW.` · `TATTOOS: AN OLD ONE DOESN'T STOP PRAYER.` · `NOT THE EASIEST VIEW. ASK WHY.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if you like, and find the nearest sound: a fan, traffic, a bird, your own breath. Stay with that one sound, then notice the quiet underneath it, the space the sound sits in. When your mind starts arguing, about music or anything else, come back to the one sound.
Ikhtilaf. Disagreement among scholars, worked out carefully from the same sources, and kept side by side rather than erased. Today's word.
Your line: where scholars differ, ask why. Not the easiest view, not the loudest: one you understand, from someone you trust. Day one hundred forty-eight, in the books.

149.title: A smile is charity
149.hook: even meeting your brother with a cheerful face is charity (Tirmidhi)
149.howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, in money and in kind, and count small acts, a smile, a kind word, directions, a helping hand, as sadaqah too.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ikhtilaf, scholars who differ, on music and on tattoos. Your line was where scholars differ, ask why.

Charity usually sounds like money. A donation page. A jar by the register. A fundraiser with a thermometer drawing that never quite fills up. If you don't have much money, it can feel like charity is for other people. Some poor companions said as much. Sahih Muslim reports they came to the Prophet ﷺ and complained: the wealthy are getting all the reward. They pray like us, they fast like us, and then they give from their extra money, and we can't. His answer widened the word.
screen: `CHARITY SOUNDS LIKE MONEY.` → `THE WEALTHY GET ALL THE REWARD.` → `HIS ANSWER WIDENED THE WORD.`

segments.voice: He told them: hasn't Allah given you things to give? Every glory to Allah is charity. Every praise is charity. Every Allahu akbar is charity. Telling someone about good is charity. The word is sadaqah, and its root is the surprising part: Lane's dictionary lists it under s-d-q, the root of sidq, truthfulness, and siddiq, the truthful. A hadith in Muslim calls sadaqah a proof, and commentators read it as faith showing it is true, faith with its hands out. In everyday use, zakat names the fixed yearly charity, which comes later this week, and sadaqah everything else: voluntary, any size, any time. And the hadith make everything else very wide. Bukhari reports: every good deed is sadaqah. Tirmidhi reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: your smile in the face of your brother is sadaqah. Pointing a lost person the right way is sadaqah. Pouring water from your bucket into someone else's is sadaqah. Sahih Muslim adds: don't think little of any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. It even says every joint in the body owes a charity each day the sun rises, and that helping a man lift his bags onto his mount pays one. So the poor companions had plenty to give after all: a face, a word, directions, a little water. The Qur'an protects the heart of it, too. Surah al-Baqarah says: A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury. A smile given freely can be worth more than a check handed over with a sneer. In these hadith, charity isn't a special occasion. It's a way of turning your face.
screen: `THE POOR COMPANIONS COMPLAIN.` · `SADAQAH — FROM THE ROOT OF TRUTH.` · `YOUR SMILE IN YOUR BROTHER'S FACE.` · `A KIND WORD, BETTER THAN ALMS WITH INJURY.` · then, large: `A FACE CAN GIVE.`

segments.voice: Picture the first person you'll see after this, and let your face soften as you meet their eyes: not a forced grin, just warmth. Then someone you tend to ignore, a cashier, a driver, a cleaner, and then someone who's difficult for you, noticing where your face tightens and letting it ease. If you pray, you can intend each smile as sadaqah.
Sadaqah. Voluntary charity, from the root of truth: any good given freely, even a cheerful face. Today's word.
Your line: a face can give. The poor companions had more to give than they thought. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 149 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CHARITY FROM THE RIGHT HAND.`

150.title: Charity from the right hand
150.hook: give so the left hand doesn't know what the right gave (Bukhari)
150.howItsDone: Muslims are encouraged to give voluntary charity quietly, without mention, following the hadith of the seven shaded and 2:271, while some scholars allow zakat to be given openly to encourage others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sadaqah, even a cheerful face. Your line was a face can give.

You've seen the photo. Someone hands a sandwich to a man sleeping on the street, and a friend films it from just the right angle. Or the charity gala where the donors' names go up on a screen, biggest first. Giving has a way of turning into a performance. One hadith goes right at the wish to be seen, with a picture so odd it's hard to forget: a left hand that has no idea what the right hand just did.
screen: `FILMED FROM THE RIGHT ANGLE.` → `NAMES ON A SCREEN, BIGGEST FIRST.` → `A LEFT HAND THAT DOESN'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: It's in Bukhari and Muslim: seven people whom Allah will shade on a day when there's no shade but His. A just ruler. A young person who grew up in worship. Someone whose heart is attached to the mosque. Two people who love each other for Allah's sake. A man called to sin by a woman of rank and beauty, who says, I fear Allah. Someone who remembered Allah alone, and whose eyes filled with tears. And the one for today: a person who gave charity and hid it, so that the left hand didn't know what the right hand gave. Your own hand, inches away, never finds out. That's how quiet it's meant to be: no photo, no mention at dinner, not even a proud glance at yourself. The Qur'an is gentle about it, not absolute. Surah al-Baqarah says that if you give openly, that is well, but if you hide it and give it to the poor, it is better for you. Open giving can encourage others, and some scholars say the yearly zakat may be given openly for that reason. But the commentators say the hidden gift protects two people: the one who receives, who keeps their dignity, and the one who gives, whose heart stays clean of showing off. The same surah warns against cancelling your charity with reminders and hurt. People tell a story, found in later collections, about Ali Zayn al-Abidin, a great-grandson of the Prophet ﷺ. For years, poor families in Medina found sacks of food at their doors at night, and never knew who brought them. When he died, they say, the deliveries stopped, and marks were found on his back from carrying them.
screen: `SEVEN IN THE SHADE.` · `THE LEFT HAND DOESN'T KNOW.` · `OPENLY IS WELL; HIDDEN IS BETTER.` · `SACKS AT THE DOOR IN THE NIGHT.` · then, large: `HIDDEN IS BEST.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who could use something, a coffee, a bag of groceries, a donation made in no one's name, and plan it so no one finds out: not them, not your friends, not your feed. Notice the little voice that wants someone to know; don't fight it or obey it; just let it be there. If you pray, you can intend it for Allah alone.
Secret charity, giving so quietly that your left hand doesn't know, one of the seven shaded on the last day.
Your line: hidden is best. Not even your left hand needs to know. One hundred fifty days now.

151.title: New to Islam
151.hook: a man pulls back his hand at the pledge; Islam wipes out what came before, and every first Muslim was new
151.howItsDone: A person becomes Muslim by saying the shahada sincerely, often before witnesses at a mosque; many mosques run classes and mentoring for new Muslims, and teachers commonly advise learning the practices step by step.

segments.voice: Yesterday: secret charity, given so quietly the left hand doesn't know. Your line was hidden is best. Today, someone walking through the door for the first time. Day one hundred fifty-one.

A man stands in front of the Prophet ﷺ to give his pledge. For years he's been on the other side. The Prophet stretches out his right hand, and the man pulls his own hand back. What's wrong, Amr? I want a condition, he says. That I be forgiven. Amr ibn al-As told this story himself, on his deathbed, and Sahih Muslim keeps it. The Prophet's answer is today's lesson, for anyone who's new. Today: shahada.
screen: `HE PULLS HIS HAND BACK.` → `A CONDITION: THAT I BE FORGIVEN.` → `TODAY, FOR ANYONE NEW.`

segments.voice: The answer was: don't you know that Islam wipes out what came before it? Whatever the past held, the pledge starts a clean page. The shahada is the sentence that does it: there is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. Said with meaning, it's how a person becomes Muslim. Some say it in a mosque after Friday prayer, to a room that breaks into Allahu akbar. Some say it quietly with a friend. People who take this step often call themselves converts, and many prefer reverts, from a hadith in Bukhari that every child is born on the fitrah, a natural sense of God. Becoming Muslim, in that picture, is coming back. Then what? New Muslims often say the hardest part is the flood: a hundred rules on day one, Arabic from strangers, a new name suggested in the parking lot. The tradition's own pace is gentler. Bukhari reports a man from Najd who asked the Prophet what Islam asks of him, and was told: the five prayers, the fast, zakat. He said: I'll do no more and no less. And the Prophet said: he has succeeded, if he's truthful. Many scholars add that a new Muslim doesn't need to change a name with a good meaning, and that Arabic comes slowly, a line at a time. And a word to those already inside. Every Muslim of the first generation was new. Khadijah, Abu Bakr, Bilal: each said the shahada for the first time, to a small community that made room for them. Tomorrow's verse even sets aside a share of zakat for hearts being drawn close.
screen: `ISLAM WIPES OUT WHAT CAME BEFORE.` · `THE SHAHADA, SAID WITH MEANING.` · `NO MORE AND NO LESS: HE SUCCEEDED.` · `EVERY FIRST MUSLIM WAS NEW.`

segments.voice: Think back to a day you were new somewhere: a school, a job, a country, someone's family kitchen, and remember who made room for you, a name, a small kindness, a seat saved. Then picture someone new in your world right now, at work, in a class, at a mosque, and picture being the one who makes room.
Shahada. The testimony: there is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. Said with meaning, it's the first step, and the first pillar. Today's word.
Your line: everyone started new. The first Muslims were all beginners, and every door has someone just walking through it. Day one hundred fifty-one, done.

152.title: The eight who receive
152.hook: the Qur'an names who zakat is for: the poor, the needy, debtors, travelers and others (9:60)
152.howItsDone: Muslims direct their zakat to the eight categories named in 9:60, often through mosques or zakat organizations, preferring local recipients, and not to their own parents or children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shahada, and a clean page for anyone new. Your line was everyone started new. Today, the verse that gives zakat its addresses, one of them for hearts being drawn close. Day one hundred fifty-two.

You've worked out the number: two and a half percent, ready to go. Now what? Hand it to the first person who asks? Drop it in any collection box? Give it to your cousin who's always broke? Most giving is left to the giver's judgment. Zakat is unusual. The Qur'an doesn't just say give. It gives you the list. One verse, in Surah at-Tawbah, names exactly who zakat is for. Eight kinds of people. Eight addresses.
screen: `THE NUMBER IS READY. NOW WHAT?` → `NOT JUST GIVE: HERE'S THE LIST.` → `EIGHT ADDRESSES.`

segments.voice: Chapter nine, verse sixty. In Pickthall's translation it begins: The alms are only for the poor and the needy. Here are all eight. One, the poor, al-fuqara'. Two, the needy, al-masakin. Scholars differ on which of the two is worse off, but together they're the people who can't cover the basics. Three, the workers who collect and manage zakat, paid from it so the system runs. Four, those whose hearts are to be reconciled: people new to Islam, or whose goodwill the community needs. Five, to free the captives. In the Prophet's time that meant helping enslaved people buy their freedom; some scholars today apply it to freeing people from captivity and trafficking. Six, the debtors, crushed by debts taken on for a decent reason. Seven, in the cause of Allah. Classically this meant those fighting in defense of the community; some modern scholars read it more widely, for example for education and dawah, and others keep it narrow. Eight, the wayfarer, stranded far from home, even if rich back there. The verse ends: a duty from Allah. Notice what the list doesn't name: the mosque's new carpet, or the giver's own family. The jurists say zakat isn't paid to your own parents or children, because you already owe them support. Bukhari reports that when the Prophet ﷺ sent Mu'adh to Yemen, he told him to take it from their rich and return it to their poor. Local, specific, human. Zakat doesn't vanish into a fog called charity. It has addresses.

segments.voice: Count the eight on your fingers, slowly, and give each a real face: the poor, the needy, the one who collects, a heart being welcomed, a captive, someone drowning in debt, the cause of Allah, a traveler stranded at a station at midnight. Go through them twice, and notice which face stays with you longest.

Your line: it has addresses. Eight fingers, eight faces, eight kinds of people. See you tomorrow.

153.title: Charity that keeps flowing
153.hook: a well, a tree, knowledge taught: good that runs after you're gone (Muslim)
153.howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqah jariyah by funding wells, planting trees, endowing schools and mosques, and teaching, and often make it on behalf of parents who have died.

segments.voice: Yesterday: zakat and the eight who receive, named in Surah at-Tawbah. Your line was it has addresses. Today, charity that outlives you. Day one hundred fifty-three.

A park bench with a small brass plate: in memory of someone nobody sitting there has met. A tree someone's grandfather planted, still shading people who don't know his name. A teacher long gone, whose way of explaining fractions is still passed from one kid to the next. Most of what people do is gone by evening. A few things keep running long after they've stopped. The hadith has a name for those things, and it's a picture of water.
screen: `A BENCH WITH A BRASS PLATE.` → `SHADE FROM A GRANDFATHER'S TREE.` → `A FEW THINGS KEEP RUNNING.`

segments.voice: Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: when a person dies, their deeds come to an end, except for three. A charity that keeps flowing. Knowledge people keep benefiting from. And a righteous child who prays for them. The first is sadaqah jariyah. Jariyah means running, flowing, like a stream: charity that keeps paying out after the giver has gone. One example is a real well. The reports say that in Medina a well called Rumah belonged to a man who sold its water, and the Muslims were short of it. The Prophet asked who would buy the well and make it free for everyone. The companion Uthman bought it, the reports in Tirmidhi say, and gave it away. People say that well still gives water today. Trees are the second picture. Bukhari and Muslim report that whenever a Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, it's charity for them, every bite, for as long as it grows. And in another report the Prophet said: if the Hour comes and one of you has a sapling in his hand, let him plant it. Even at the end of the world, plant. Over the centuries, Muslims turned this into institutions: endowments called waqf that paid for hospitals, schools, public fountains and travelers' inns, some still running long after their founders died. But it doesn't need to be big. Teaching a child to read is flowing knowledge. A recipe passed on. A tree in a yard. Something you start that keeps going without you.
screen: `THREE THINGS KEEP RUNNING.` · `JARIYAH — FLOWING, LIKE A STREAM.` · `UTHMAN BUYS THE WELL OF RUMAH.` · `A SAPLING IN YOUR HAND AT THE END.` · then, large: `THE WELL KEEPS GIVING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you do well, cooking a dish, fixing a bike, reciting a short surah, writing a letter, calming a crying baby, and one person who'd be helped by learning it. Or picture a seed going into soil, in a pot, a yard or a community garden, and the shade it might give when you're not there. If you pray, you can intend one of them as sadaqah jariyah.
Sadaqah jariyah. Flowing charity: a well, a tree, knowledge taught, good that keeps running after you're gone. Today's word.
Your line: the well keeps giving. Some good keeps running without you. Day one hundred fifty-three.

154.title: The neighbor
154.hook: Jibril kept urging kindness to the neighbor until the Prophet ﷺ thought neighbors would inherit (Bukhari)
154.tomorrow: Removing a stone from the road
154.howItsDone: Muslims give special weight to neighbors, of any faith: sharing food, visiting, helping and avoiding any harm to them, following the hadith of Jibril and the neighbor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sadaqah jariyah, the well, the tree and the knowledge that keep running. Your line was the well keeps giving. Today, where charity starts. Day one hundred fifty-four.

Quick question: what's the name of the person who lives closest to you? Not your closest friend. The closest person: the other side of your wall, across the hall, next door. A lot of people don't know. They know strangers across the world by their usernames, and nod at the person ten feet away without ever learning a name. They send money to causes overseas, which is good, and have never knocked on the door beside theirs. In Islam, charity has a starting point, and it's on the other side of your wall.
screen: `WHO LIVES CLOSEST TO YOU?` → `A NOD, TEN FEET AWAY.` → `CHARITY HAS A STARTING POINT.`

segments.voice: Bukhari and Muslim report the Prophet ﷺ saying: Jibril kept urging me to be good to the neighbor, so much that I thought he would make the neighbor an heir. An heir: someone with a legal share in what you leave behind, like family. That's how often the angel came back to it. The Qur'an names neighbors in Surah an-Nisa, in a list of those to be good to: parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is related to you and the neighbor who is a stranger, the companion at your side. And Bukhari reports a warning so strong the Prophet said it three times: by Allah, he does not believe. Who? The one whose neighbor is not safe from his harm. The hadith get practical. Sahih Muslim reports him telling the companion Abu Dharr: when you make a stew, add extra water, and look to your neighbors. Stretch the pot. Bukhari reports him telling women not to think any gift to a neighbor too small, even a sheep's hoof. And a neighbor isn't defined by faith. Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud report that the companion Abdullah ibn Amr had a sheep slaughtered, and when he came home the first thing he asked was: have you given some to our Jewish neighbor? He had heard the Prophet's words about Jibril and the neighbor. Scholars have argued over how far a neighborhood stretches. The principle is simpler than any measuring. Before the world, the house next door. Before the cause, the name.
screen: `JIBRIL KEPT URGING.` · `BY ALLAH, HE DOES NOT BELIEVE.` · `ADD WATER TO THE STEW.` · `HAVE YOU GIVEN TO OUR JEWISH NEIGHBOR?` · then, large: `START NEXT DOOR.`

segments.voice: Picture the doors nearest yours, one by one, and notice which neighbors you know and which you don't. Pick one, and picture something small you could bring: extra from dinner, a few pieces of fruit, a note with your name and number, even just a hello, since no gift is too small, not even a sheep's hoof. Picture knocking, and their face, and if it makes you nervous, breathe through it.
The neighbor. The one next door, whose rights Jibril urged so often the Prophet thought they would inherit. Today's word.
Your line: start next door. Jibril kept coming back to the neighbor. That's day one hundred fifty-four.
